title: Technical Communication
summary: Your code ships once; your writing gets re-read for years. The skill that gets engineers promoted is explaining what they built and why.

blocks.markdown:
Technical communication moves an idea from your head into someone else's, accurately, with the least effort on their side.

- **One skill, many forms** — docs, design docs, PRs, commits, Slack, and a 2-minute exec update are all the same move.
- **Write for the reader** — they're busy, missing context, and skimming. Do their thinking-work for them.
- **Teams are bottlenecked by communication**, not typing speed. The model in your head is invisible until you write it down.
- Writing is the **cache that survives restarts** — memory and meetings don't.

blocks.subTitle: Match artifact to the job
blocks.markdown:
Pick the artifact by lifespan and stakes, not by habit.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Durable decision with buy-in | Design doc / RFC |
| Quick, low-stakes clarification | Slack / async |
| High ambiguity or conflict | Sync call |
| Explaining a code change | PR + commits |
| Status to leadership | 3-sentence update |

blocks.subTitle: The design doc / RFC
blocks.markdown:
A design doc is a written proposal you write **before** building, reviewed by the people it affects.

![Structure of a good design doc](assets/d10-technical-communication/design-doc-structure.svg)

- Canonical order: **context** (problem, why now), **goals / non-goals**, **proposed design**, **alternatives considered**, **risks**, **rollout / rollback**.
- Context comes before solution, always — reviewers read top to bottom.
- An **RFC** is the same skeleton run through heavier, often public review. Small teams say "design doc."

assets.alt: Structure of a good design doc

blocks.subTitle: Why write the doc at all
blocks.markdown:
You write the doc to find the bugs in your plan, then let others find the ones you missed.

- In your head ideas feel coherent; **writing them down makes the gaps scream.**
- **Non-goals** kill scope creep and pre-empt "but what about X?" — naming one is a gift to your reviewer.
- **Alternatives considered** separate a senior doc from a junior one: list the real options and why you rejected each.
- Getting buy-in is a side effect, not the point.

blocks.subTitle: The RFC lifecycle
blocks.markdown:
An RFC isn't just a document — it's a document moving through states.

![RFC lifecycle from draft to implemented](assets/d10-technical-communication/rfc-lifecycle.svg)

- **Draft** the author writes, then **In Review** where the team gives feedback and the doc loops back for revisions.
- It ends **Accepted** (then implemented) or **Rejected / withdrawn**.
- Most of the value and most of the time live in the **review loop**, not the final state.

assets.alt: RFC lifecycle from draft to implemented

blocks.subTitle: BLUF & the inverted pyramid
blocks.markdown:
Lead with the answer — the decision or ask goes in sentence one, justification after.

- Journalists call it the **inverted pyramid**: most important first, supporting detail below, nice-to-know last.
- Engineers call the top line **BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front.**
- A reader spends ~10 seconds deciding whether to keep going. A conclusion in paragraph six is a conclusion nobody reads.
- It feels backwards to write because you discovered the conclusion **last** — which is exactly why people get it wrong.

blocks.subTitle: Commit messages & PRs
blocks.markdown:
The diff already shows **what** changed; the message's entire job is the **why**.

- A commit is read by someone six months out running `git blame`, trying to understand a line before they dare touch it.
- Good shape: a **≤50-char imperative summary** ("Fix race in token refresh"), blank line, then a why-focused body.
- A PR description adds: what it does, why, how to test it, and any risk.
- See [d09-code-review-collaboration](d09-code-review-collaboration.md) for the reviewing side.

blocks.subTitle: Async vs sync
blocks.markdown:
Async scales; sync resolves. Default to async, switch to sync to resolve.

| Aspect | Async (doc, PR) | Sync (meeting) |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | ~3 min to write | 3+ person-hours |
| Record | Searchable | Vanishes |
| Best for | Most decisions | Ambiguity, conflict |

Text escalates conflict; voice de-escalates it. After any sync decision, **write it down async** — or the team never learns it.

blocks.subTitle: Up vs across
blocks.markdown:
Same facts, different altitude depending on the audience.

- **Up (leadership)** → lead with the **decision, risk, cost, timeline**. They want to know if it's on track and whether to act.
- **Across (peers)** → lead with **design, trade-offs, correctness**. They want enough to build against it or catch your mistakes.
- Burying the ask under mechanism reads as "doesn't know what matters."
- The other levers: author effort beats reader effort (many readers), and **layer** detail rather than cutting it.

blocks.subTitle: Real cultures
blocks.markdown:
The big shops bet hard on writing forcing clear thinking.

- **Google** — institutionalized the design doc as the reviewable unit of thought, so design mistakes get caught cheap.
- **IETF / Rust** — numbered, public RFCs leave an auditable trail of *why* a protocol or language is the way it is.
- **Amazon** — banned slides for **6-page narratives** read silently; prose exposes the gaps bullets hide.
- **Conventional Commits** — standardized messages because `git blame` makes them a permanent explanation layer.

blocks.subTitle: Signals it's working
blocks.markdown:
Communication has no dashboard, but it has tells.

- **Good** — reviewers engage the *substance*, not "what is this even about?"
- **Good** — decisions stay decided; someone links your old doc to settle a new argument.
- **Good** — people act from your writing without pinging you; on-call resolves from the runbook.
- **Bad** — "quick sync" load keeps climbing, and `git blame` lands on a line whose message is just "fix."

The mistakes that quietly cost weeks:

- **"The code is self-documenting."** Code shows *what*, never *why* you chose it or what you ruled out — and the why is what evaporates.
- **"More detail = better."** No: more *relevant, ordered* detail. Fix completeness vs readability by **layering**, not dumping.
- **"The doc is just sign-off overhead."** Approval is the side effect; the value is finding holes before you code.
- **"Write it in the order I figured it out."** That order is full of dead ends. Organize around the reader; lead with the conclusion.
- **"A meeting will be faster."** Faster for the organizer, costly for the group, and it leaves no searchable record.
